questions.questionText: Which of the following is not a coordination compound?
questions.explanation: Urea, (NH2)2CO, is a simple organic diamide consisting solely of main-group elements without a central metal coordination center.
questions.notes: Urea is an organic diamide, not a metal coordination compound.
questions.caveat: In contrast, haemoglobin contains an iron porphyrin complex, chlorophyll contains magnesium, and cobalt(III) ammines are classic Werner coordination complexes.

questions.questionText: The number of chlorine atoms acting as ligands in the complex [Co(en)2(H2)Cl]Cl2 is:
questions.explanation: Ligands reside within the inner coordination sphere enclosed by the square brackets. In [Co(en)2(H2)Cl]Cl2, only 1 chlorine atom is inside the brackets acting as a chlorido ligand, while the 2 chloride atoms outside serve as counteranions.
questions.notes: Only the single Cl atom inside the square brackets acts as an inner-sphere ligand.

questions.questionText: Consider the complex [Co(NH3)5CO3]ClO4, in which coordination number, oxidation number, and the number of d-electrons on the metal are respectively?
questions.explanation: In [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]ClO4, the cobalt center is coordinated to five monodentate NH3 ligands and one monodentate carbonato ligand, giving a coordination number of 6. Balancing charges with perchlorate (ClO4-) and carbonato (CO3 2-) gives Co3+ (x - 2 = +1 => x = +3). Neutral cobalt is [Ar] 4s2 3d7, so Co3+ has 6 d-electrons ([Ar] 3d6).
questions.notes: Coordination number = 6; Co(III) oxidation state; d6 configuration.

questions.questionText: Which of the following compound shows both linkage and ionization isomerism?
questions.explanation: [Co(NO2)Br(NH3)4]Cl contains the ambidentate NO2- ligand capable of binding via N (nitro) or O (nitrito), conferring linkage isomerism. It also possesses different anions inside and outside the sphere (inner Br-, outer Cl-), allowing ion exchange to yield the ionization isomer [Co(NO2)Cl(NH3)4]Br.
questions.notes: Shows linkage isomerism via NO2/ONO and ionization isomerism via Br-/Cl- exchange.
questions.caveat: Shows linkage isomerism via NO2/ONO and ionization isomerism via Br-/Cl- exchange.

questions.questionText: The complex [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 will give white precipitate with:
questions.explanation: In [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4, sulfate (SO4 2-) is the free counteranion in solution. When treated with a lead(II) salt like PbCl2, Pb2+ reacts with free SO4 2- to precipitate insoluble white lead(II) sulfate (PbSO4). Silver nitrate does not precipitate because bromide is coordinated inside the inner sphere.
questions.notes: Free sulfate precipitates with Pb2+ as insoluble white PbSO4.

questions.questionText: The name of the coordination compound [Cu(NH3)4](NO3)2 is:
questions.explanation: Under IUPAC rules, the complex cation [Cu(NH3)4]2+ is named without a space as tetraamminecopper(II), followed by the counteranion "nitrate" without any Greek multiplying prefix ("dinitrate"), making tetraamminecopper(II) nitrate the correct systematic name.
questions.notes: No multiplying prefix on counterion nitrate; no space within complex cation name.

questions.questionText: The name of [Fe(CN)2(CH3NH2)2] is:
questions.explanation: The neutral ligand CH3NH2 is methylamine. In IUPAC naming, ligands with compound names use the multiplicative prefix "bis-", and anionic ligands are named first (dicyano). The iron atom is in the +2 oxidation state, yielding dicyanobis(methylamine)iron(II).
questions.notes: Multiplicative prefix bis- is required for the substituted amine ligand methylamine.

questions.questionText: The name of [Pt(NH3)4Cl2][PtCl4] is:
questions.explanation: In the cation [Pt(NH3)4Cl2]2+, ligands are listed alphabetically: "ammine" precedes "dichloro", and Pt is in the +4 oxidation state. In the anion [PtCl4]2-, Pt is in the +2 state and named tetrachloroplatinate(II). Naming the cation first gives tetraamminedichloroplatinum(IV) tetrachloroplatinate(II).
questions.notes: Ligands arranged alphabetically: tetraammine before dichloro; cation named before anion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following coordination complexes is most stable?
questions.explanation: Ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA4-) is a hexadentate chelating ligand that wraps around the metal center forming five fused five-membered chelate rings. The massive entropic gain upon displacing six monodentate water molecules confers extraordinary thermodynamic stability (log Kf ≈ 18.6) to [NiEDTA]2-.
questions.notes: Hexadentate EDTA chelate effect produces the highest thermodynamic stability constant.

questions.questionText: SCN- has two possible donor atoms. It is a/an
questions.explanation: Although the thiocyanate ion (SCN-) possesses two potential donor atoms (sulfur and nitrogen), geometric constraints prevent it from binding simultaneously to the same metal center. It coordinates through only one donor atom at a time, classifying it as a monodentate (specifically ambidentate) ligand.
questions.notes: SCN- binds via either S or N, but only one at a time, making it monodentate.

questions.questionText: Which of the following gives the most number of isomers?
questions.explanation: [Cr(SCN)2(NH3)4]4+ has cis and trans geometrical isomers, and each geometry can have three distinct linkage combinations for the two ambidentate thiocyanate ligands: (-SCN,-SCN), (-SCN,-NCS), and (-NCS,-NCS), producing 6 distinct isomers, the highest among the choices.
questions.notes: 2 geometrical arrangements x 3 linkage combinations = 6 isomers.
questions.caveat: 2 geometrical arrangements x 3 linkage combinations = 6 isomers.

questions.questionText: [Co(NH3)4(NO2)2]Cl exhibits:
questions.explanation: This complex shows linkage isomerism (NO2/ONO), geometrical isomerism (cis and trans [Ma4b2]), and ionization isomerism (exchange of inner NO2- with outer Cl- to give [Co(NH3)4Cl(NO2)]NO2). Because both cis and trans [Ma4b2] have mirror planes of symmetry, optical isomerism is absent, making D correct.
questions.notes: Optical isomerism is impossible for [Ma4b2] complexes because both cis and trans isomers have planes of symmetry.
questions.caveat: Optical isomerism is impossible for [Ma4b2] complexes because both cis and trans isomers have planes of symmetry.

questions.questionText: The total number of possible isomers for the square planar [PtCl(NO2)(NO3)(SCN)]2- is:
questions.explanation: A square planar complex with four different monodentate ligands [Mabcd] forms exactly 3 geometrical isomers. Among the four ligands, NO2- has 2 linkage modes (N, O) and SCN- has 2 linkage modes (S, N). Multiplying 3 geometrical arrangements by 2 (NO2) and 2 (SCN) gives 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 total isomers.
questions.notes: 3 geometrical isomers x 2 linkage (NO2) x 2 linkage (SCN) = 12 total isomers.
questions.caveat: 3 geometrical isomers x 2 linkage (NO2) x 2 linkage (SCN) = 12 total isomers.

questions.questionText: Optical isomers have:

options.C: difference in action towards plane polarized light

questions.explanation: Enantiomers share the same molecular formula and identical scalar physical properties (such as melting point, boiling point, density, and solubility in achiral solvents), but rotate the plane of polarized light in equal magnitude but opposite directions. Therefore, all of the statements are correct.
questions.notes: Enantiomers have identical achiral physical properties and rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.

questions.questionText: Which of the following compound shows optical isomerism?
questions.explanation: The tris(oxalato)chromate(III) ion, [Cr(C2O4)3]3-, has D3 point group symmetry like a three-bladed propeller. It lacks any improper rotation axis (no plane of symmetry or inversion center) and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers (Δ and Λ), demonstrating optical isomerism.
questions.notes: [Cr(C2O4)3]3- is a chiral tris-chelate showing optical activity.
questions.caveat: [Cr(C2O4)3]3- is a chiral tris-chelate showing optical activity.

questions.questionText:
Two complexes given below are:
(Shown in accompanying diagram: two representations of cis-[M(en)2A2] drawn with octahedral frames in different spatial orientations)
questions.explanation: In both depictions, the two monodentate ligands A are mutually cis (at 90 degrees), and the two chelating ethylenediamine (en) rings occupy the remaining four cis-coordinated positions. Rotating the first drawing by 90 degrees around an axis brings all atoms into identical spatial alignment with the second drawing; hence, they represent the identical complex.
questions.notes: The two figures depict the same cis isomer in different orientations, superimposable by simple rigid-body rotation.
questions.caveat: The two figures depict the same cis isomer in different orientations, superimposable by simple rigid-body rotation.

questions.questionText:
Which of the following will have two stereoisomeric forms?
i. [Cr(NO3)3(NH3)3]
ii. K3[Fe(C2O4)3]
iii. [CoCl2(en)2]+
iv. [CoBrCl(ox)2]3-
questions.explanation: Complex i [Ma3b3] forms exactly two geometrical isomers: facial (fac) and meridional (mer), both achiral. Complex ii [M(A-A)3] forms exactly two optical isomers: the Δ and Λ enantiomeric pair.
questions.notes: i has 2 geometrical isomers (fac/mer); ii has 2 optical enantiomers (Δ/Λ); iii has 3 stereoisomers.
questions.caveat: In contrast, complex iii forms three stereoisomers (trans and a pair of cis enantiomers). Thus, only i and ii have exactly two stereoisomeric forms.

questions.questionText: The octahedral complex CoSO4Cl5NH3 exists in two isomeric forms X and Y. Isomer X reacts with AgNO3 to give a white precipitate, but does not react with BaCl2. Isomer Y gives white precipitate with BaCl2 but does not react with AgNO3. Isomers X and Y are:
questions.explanation: Isomer X reacts with AgNO3 to precipitate AgCl, meaning Cl- is the outer-sphere counterion: [Co(SO4)(NH3)5]Cl. Isomer Y reacts with BaCl2 to precipitate BaSO4, meaning SO4 2- is the counterion: [CoCl(NH3)5]SO4. Interchange of an anionic ligand with an outer counterion defines ionization isomerism.
questions.notes: Ionization isomers differing in which anion acts as the free counterion in aqueous solution.
questions.caveat: Ionization isomers differing in which anion acts as the free counterion in aqueous solution.

questions.questionText: Which of the following does not have optical isomer?
questions.explanation: [Co(NH3)3Cl3] is an [Ma3b3] complex that exists as facial (fac) and meridional (mer) geometrical isomers. The fac isomer possesses three planes of symmetry (C3v), and the mer isomer possesses a mirror plane of symmetry (C2v). Having planes of symmetry, neither isomer is chiral, so it has no optical isomers.
questions.notes: Both fac and mer forms of [Ma3b3] contain mirror planes and are strictly achiral.

questions.questionText: Number of geometrical isomers shown by the octahedral complex of the type [MX2Y4] is
questions.explanation: An octahedral complex with formula [MX2Y4] has exactly two geometrical arrangements for the two X ligands: cis, in which the two X ligands subtend an angle of 90 degrees at the metal center, and trans, in which they occupy opposite vertices at 180 degrees.
questions.notes: Exactly 2 geometrical isomers: cis and trans.
questions.caveat: Exactly 2 geometrical isomers: cis and trans.

questions.questionText: Transition metals form most stable complex ions as:

options.B: they have large charge to radius ratio
options.C: vacant orbitals to accommodate electrons are present

questions.explanation: The propensity of transition metals to form exceptionally stable complexes stems collectively from their high charge density (large charge-to-radius ratio), their variable oxidation states allowing favorable redox tuning, and the presence of low-lying empty valence d-orbitals suitable for accepting ligand electron pairs.
questions.notes: All listed properties contribute synergistically to complex stability in transition metals.

questions.questionText: Which of the following metal atomic orbital is considered in crystal field theory?
questions.explanation: Classic Crystal Field Theory focuses exclusively on the effect of the surrounding electrostatic ligand field on the five degenerate valence d orbitals of transition metal ions, describing how their energies split without considering s or p orbital hybridization.
questions.notes: CFT specifically addresses the energetic perturbation and splitting of d-orbitals.

questions.questionText: The more stable complex among the following is:
questions.explanation: Iron(III) carries a +3 charge and has a significantly smaller ionic radius (64.5 pm) than divalent Fe2+ (78 pm) or Mn2+ (83 pm). Its much higher charge density creates stronger electrostatic attraction and greater covalent orbital overlap with water ligands, giving [Fe(H2O)6]3+ the highest stability.
questions.notes: Fe3+ has much higher charge density than the divalent cations, maximizing thermodynamic stability.

questions.questionText: Stability of a metal complex depends upon:

options.A: charge on the central metal ion

questions.explanation: The overall thermodynamic stability of a coordination complex depends on metal properties (higher charge and smaller radius increase stability), ligand properties (basicity, polarizability, and spectrochemical strength), and chelation (multidentate ring formation increases stability via entropy). Hence, all of the above factors are critical.
questions.notes: Metal charge, ligand properties, and chelate formation all govern complex stability.

questions.questionText: The stability constant of the complexes formed by a metal ion M2+ with NH3, CN-, H2O, and en are of the order of 10^11, 10^27, 10^15, and 10^18, respectively. Which of the following is true:

options.C: these values cannot predict the strength of the ligand
options.D: all the ligands are equally strong

questions.explanation: The stability constant (Kf) directly quantifies the thermodynamic equilibrium for complex formation. A formation constant of order 10^27 for the cyanide complex is by far the largest value among the four ligands, establishing that CN- binds most strongly to the M2+ ion.
questions.notes: Kf of 10^27 demonstrates that CN- forms the most thermodynamically stable complex.

questions.questionText:
The degeneracy of d-orbitals is lost under:
i. strong field ligand
ii. weak field ligand
iii. mixed field ligand
iv. chelated ligand field
questions.explanation: The degeneracy of the five metal d-orbitals is lifted whenever ligands approach the central metal ion in any non-spherical coordination geometry. Whether the ligands are strong field, weak field, mixed, or chelating, their anisotropic electrostatic and covalent interactions inevitably break the five-fold d degeneracy.
questions.notes: Any non-spherical field (strong, weak, mixed, or chelated) lifts the 5-fold d orbital degeneracy.

questions.questionText: Choose the incorrect order of stability:
questions.explanation: The official answer key explicitly designates the parenthesised alternative (B/D) for this question. In option B, NO2- is a stronger-field and more stable ligand than NH3, making the sequence incorrect. In option D, a divalent Rh(II) aqua ion is placed between two trivalent ions (Co3+ and Ir3+), violating periodic and oxidation-state stability trends. Both B and D depict incorrect stability orders.
questions.notes: The official answer key designates parenthesised alternative (B/D). Both option B and option D show flawed stability orders, so both answers are accepted.

questions.questionText: The complexes formed by Cu2+ ion are more stable than those formed by Cd2+ ion because:

options.A: the value of the stability constant for Cd2+ complexes is greater than that of Cu2+ ions
options.B: the charge density on Cu2+ is greater than that of Cd2+ ion
options.C: the ionic radius of Cu2+ ion is more than that of Cd2+ ion

questions.explanation: Although both Cu2+ and Cd2+ carry a +2 formal charge, the 3d transition metal ion Cu2+ has a much smaller ionic radius (~73 pm) than the 4d metal ion Cd2+ (~95 pm). Consequently, Cu2+ possesses a substantially greater charge density (charge-to-radius ratio), leading to stronger electrostatic and covalent bond strengths.
questions.notes: Smaller ionic radius of Cu2+ gives higher charge density, explaining its higher stability.

questions.questionText: The most stable complex species is:
questions.explanation: The official answer key marks (A/B) as accepted alternatives. Chemically, [Fe(C2O4)3]3- derives immense thermodynamic stability from the chelate effect (three bidentate rings), whereas [Fe(CN)6]3- exhibits massive stability from strong-field covalent σ-bonding and π-backbonding with iron(III). Both represent exceptionally stable complex species.
questions.notes: The official answer key designates parenthesised alternative (A/B). Both the chelated tris(oxalato) complex (A) and hexacyanidoferrate(III) (B) are accepted.

questions.questionText: In Fe(CO)5, the Fe-C bond possesses:
questions.explanation: In metal carbonyls like Fe(CO)5, bonding is synergic: CO donates its lone pair into empty iron hybrid orbitals to form a σ-bond, while filled iron d orbitals donate electron density into the empty π* orbitals of CO (π-backbonding). The Fe-C bond thus possesses both σ and π character.
questions.notes: Synergic bonding in metal carbonyls involves both sigma and pi character.

questions.questionText: In the complex ion ML6 n+ ,Mn+ has five d-electrons and L is weak field ligand. According to crystal field theory, how many unpaired electrons are there in this complex ion?
questions.explanation: With a weak-field ligand, the crystal field splitting Δo is smaller than the electron pairing energy (Δo < P), resulting in a high-spin complex. For a d5 system, electrons occupy all five d-orbitals singly according to Hund's rule: configuration t2g^3 eg^2, giving exactly 5 unpaired electrons.
questions.notes: High-spin d5 has one electron in each of the 5 d-orbitals, giving 5 unpaired electrons.

questions.questionText: The energies of dxy and dz2 orbitals in octahedral and tetrahedral transition metal complexes are such that:

options.A: E(dxy) > E(dz2) in both tetrahedral and octahedral complexes
options.B: E(dxy) < E(dz2) in both tetrahedral and octahedral complexes
options.C: E(dxy) > E(dz2) in tetrahedral but E(dxy) < E(dz2) in octahedral complexes
options.D: E(dxy) < E(dz2) in tetrahedral but E(dxy) < E(dz2) in octahedral complexes

questions.explanation: In octahedral geometry, dz2 belongs to the higher-energy eg set pointing directly at ligands, whereas dxy is in the lower-energy t2g set, so E(dxy) < E(dz2). In tetrahedral geometry, the splitting pattern is reversed: t2 (including dxy) is higher in energy than the e set (including dz2), so E(dxy) > E(dz2).
questions.notes: In Oh: E(dxy) < E(dz2); in Td: E(dxy) > E(dz2).

questions.questionText: What is the electronic arrangement of metal atom/ion in octahedral complex with d4 configuration, if Δo < pairing energy
questions.explanation: When Δo is smaller than the pairing energy, electrons prefer promoting to the higher-energy eg level rather than pairing in t2g. For a d4 metal ion, three electrons occupy the three degenerate t2g orbitals singly and the fourth electron enters the eg set, producing the high-spin configuration t2g^3 eg^1.
questions.notes: Δo < P produces high-spin t2g3 eg1.

questions.questionText: The ratio of CFSE for [NiCl6]4- and [NiCl4]2- will be nearly:
questions.explanation: Both complexes contain Ni(II), a d8 ion. For octahedral [NiCl6]4-, CFSE_oct = 1.2 Δo. For tetrahedral [NiCl4]2-, CFSE_tet = 0.8 Δt = 0.8 * (4/9)Δo = (16/45)Δo. Taking the ratio gives CFSE_oct / CFSE_tet = 1.2 / (16/45) = (6/5) * (45/16) = 27/8.

questions.questionText: The d orbitals that are stabilized in an octahedral magnetic field are:
questions.explanation: In an octahedral field, ligands approach along the x, y, and z axes. The t2g orbitals (dxy, dxz, and dyz/dyx) have lobes pointing between the Cartesian axes, experiencing less electrostatic repulsion and becoming stabilized by 0.4Δo relative to the barycenter.
questions.notes: The t2g set (dxy, dxz, dyz) points between the axes and is stabilized by 0.4Δo.

questions.questionText: The magnitude of crystal field stabilization energy in tetrahedral complexes is considerably less than in the octahedral field because:

options.A: there are only four ligands instead of six
options.B: the direction of the orbitals does not coincide with the direction of the ligands

questions.explanation: The crystal field splitting in tetrahedral geometry is related to octahedral splitting by Δt = 4/9 Δo. This substantial reduction arises from two physical factors: having only 4 ligands instead of 6 (giving a factor of 4/6 = 2/3) and the fact that tetrahedral ligand trajectories do not point directly at any d orbital (giving another geometric factor of 2/3). Thus, both points are correct.
questions.notes: Δt = (2/3) * (2/3) * Δo = 4/9 Δo, combining fewer ligands and indirect orbital orientation.

questions.questionText: Which of the following on CO ligand is true?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide coordinates through the lone pair on carbon by donating electron density into an empty metal hybrid orbital (σ-donation), while simultaneously accepting electron density from filled metal d-orbitals into its low-energy empty π* antibonding orbitals (π-backbonding). Thus, CO is a σ-donor and π-acceptor.
questions.notes: Synergic bonding classifies CO as a sigma-donor and pi-acceptor.

questions.questionText: Cisplatin compounds are used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is an inorganic platinum-based chemotherapeutic drug widely used in the clinical treatment of various cancers, where it binds to DNA to form intrastrand crosslinks that inhibit DNA replication and trigger apoptosis in malignant cells.
questions.notes: Classic platinum anticancer chemotherapeutic.

questions.questionText: In the spectrochemical series, which ligand produces strongest field?
questions.explanation: In the spectrochemical series, ligands are ordered by the magnitude of crystal field splitting Δo they induce: I- < Br- < Cl- < F- < OH- < H2O < NH3 < NO2- < CN- < CO. Carbon monoxide is the strongest π-acceptor ligand and sits at the highest end of the series, producing the strongest crystal field.
questions.notes: CO is at the extreme strong-field end of the spectrochemical series.

questions.questionText: Which effect/theory could account for the presence of two different M-L bond lengths in [Cu(H2O)6]2+?
questions.explanation: Cu(II) has a d9 electronic configuration with an unevenly occupied degenerate eg level (t2g^6 eg^3). According to the Jahn-Teller theorem, any non-linear molecule in a degenerate electronic state must undergo geometric distortion to remove degeneracy and lower the overall energy, resulting in four short equatorial and two long axial Cu-O bonds.
questions.notes: Jahn-Teller distortion in d9 copper(II) causes tetragonal elongation (two distinct bond lengths).

questions.questionText: Which of the coordination compounds will give exactly three isomers?
questions.explanation: [Co(en)2Cl2]Cl exists as a trans isomer (which has an inversion center and is optically inactive) and a cis isomer (which lacks a plane or center of inversion and exists as a pair of non-superimposable optical enantiomers: Δ and Λ). Together, these constitute exactly 3 stereoisomers.
questions.notes: Trans isomer (1) + cis enantiomeric pair (2) = 3 stereoisomers.
questions.caveat: Trans isomer (1) + cis enantiomeric pair (2) = 3 stereoisomers.

questions.questionText: Hybridization involves:

options.B: combination and redistribution of atomic orbitals

questions.explanation: Hybridization is defined as the quantum-mechanical mixing, combination, and spatial redistribution of atomic orbitals with similar energies to form new equivalent hybrid orbitals with specific directional geometries suitable for bonding.
questions.notes: Fundamental definition of orbital hybridization in chemical bonding theory.

questions.questionText: The name of [Ni(NH3)4][NiCl4] is:
questions.explanation: In a salt containing complex cation and anion, both nickel centers are in the +2 oxidation state ([Ni(NH3)4]2+ and [NiCl4]2-). The cation is named tetraamminenickel(II) and the anion uses the suffix "-ate" as tetrachloronickelate(II).
questions.notes: Anionic complex receives -ate suffix; both nickel centers have oxidation state +2.

questions.questionText: The name of K3[Ir(C2O4)3] is:
questions.explanation: For the bidentate chelating ligand oxalato, the IUPAC rules prefer the multiplicative prefix "tris(oxalato)". Because the complex is an anion [Ir(C2O4)3]3-, the iridium center is named iridate(III), yielding potassium tris(oxalato)iridate(III).
questions.notes: Tris prefix for bidentate oxalate; anionic metal name ends in -ate.

questions.questionText: Which of the following octahedral complexes will have the highest Δo?
questions.explanation: According to the spectrochemical series, cyanide (CN-) is one of the strongest field ligands due to its potent π-acceptor capability. Therefore, [Co(CN)6]3- exhibits a substantially larger crystal field splitting parameter (Δo) than complexes with ammine, aqua, or chloride ligands.
questions.notes: CN- is at the strong-field end of the spectrochemical series, maximizing Δo.

questions.questionText: How many isomer(s) is/are possible for a tetrahedral complex with the formula [M(A-A)2]? Note that A-A refers to a symmetrical bidentate ligand.
questions.explanation: In a tetrahedral complex [M(A-A)2] with symmetrical chelating ligands (such as bis(acetylacetonato) or bis(oxalato)), the geometry possesses D2d point group symmetry. This symmetry includes an improper rotation axis S4 and mirror planes, precluding both geometrical and optical isomerism; thus, only 1 unique isomer exists.
questions.notes: Symmetrical bis-chelate tetrahedral complex is achiral (D2d) with no cis/trans isomers.
questions.caveat: Symmetrical bis-chelate tetrahedral complex is achiral (D2d) with no cis/trans isomers.

questions.questionText: Which of the following has the highest molar conductivity?
questions.explanation: Molar electrical conductivity of an electrolyte solution increases with the total number of ions produced per formula unit and their ionic charges. [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 dissociates into 4 ions (one [Co(NH3)6]3+ tri-cation and three Cl- anions), giving the highest conductance among all options.
questions.notes: Produces 4 ions in solution (1:3 electrolyte), giving the highest conductivity.

questions.questionText: The ionization isomer of [Cr(H2O)4Cl(NO2)]Cl is:
questions.explanation: Ionization isomers result from the exchange of an anionic ligand inside the coordination sphere with an outer-sphere counterion. Exchanging inner NO2- with outer Cl- gives [Cr(H2O)4Cl2](NO2), which releases nitrite rather than chloride in aqueous solution.
questions.notes: Option B is a linkage isomer; option C is a hydrate isomer.
questions.caveat: Option B is a linkage isomer; option C is a hydrate isomer.

questions.questionText: The C-O bond length of CO ligand increases as we change the central metal ion from a d0 species to a d1 species. Assuming that the ion radii and oxidation states of both species are the same, the observation is due to:
questions.explanation: Introducing a d electron into the metal valence shell enables metal-to-ligand π-backbonding into the empty antibonding π* orbitals of the carbonyl ligand. Populating these π* antibonding molecular orbitals weakens the C-O bond and lengthens the carbon-oxygen distance.
questions.notes: Electron density into pi*(CO) weakens the internal C-O bond, increasing its bond length.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: E(dxy) > E(dz2) in both tetrahedral and octahedral complexes
options.B: E(dxy) < E(dz2) in both square planar and octahedral complexes
options.C: E(dxy) > E(dz2) in tetrahedral but E(dxy) < E(dz2) in octahedral complexes
options.D: E(dxy) < E(dz2) in square planar but E(dxy) < E(dz2) in octahedral complexes

questions.explanation: In octahedral complexes, dz2 belongs to the higher-energy eg set pointing at ligands, while dxy is in the lower-energy t2g set, so E(dxy) < E(dz2). In tetrahedral complexes, the splitting is inverted: t2 (including dxy) is higher in energy than the e set (including dz2), meaning E(dxy) > E(dz2).
questions.notes: In Oh: t2g (dxy) < eg (dz2); in Td: e (dz2) < t2 (dxy).

questions.questionText: Cisplatin compounds are used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Cisplatin, cis-diamminedichloroplatinum(II), is a widely utilized chemotherapy medication used in the clinical treatment of various cancers, including testicular, ovarian, and lung cancers, by crosslinking purine bases in DNA.
questions.notes: Well-known platinum-based anticancer therapeutic agent.

questions.questionText: Which of the following isomerisms comprise of metal complex isomers with different general molecular formula?
questions.explanation: By definition, all isomers must have the exact same chemical composition and molecular formula, differing only in the connectivity or spatial arrangement of atoms. Since no valid isomerism involves complexes with different molecular formulas, "none of the above" is correct.
questions.notes: Isomers must share identical molecular formulas by chemical definition.
questions.caveat: Isomers must share identical molecular formulas by chemical definition.

questions.questionText: [Cu(SCN)2(NH3)4] is an octahedral complex. How many isomers are possible for this molecular formula?
questions.explanation: For an octahedral [Ma4b2] complex, there are 2 geometrical arrangements: cis and trans. The two thiocyanate ligands can coordinate in three distinct linkage combinations: (SCN, SCN), (NCS, NCS), and (SCN, NCS). Combining 2 geometries x 3 linkage combinations produces 6 total isomers.
questions.notes: 3 linkage modes (S/S, N/N, S/N) x 2 geometrical isomers (cis/trans) = 6 isomers.
questions.caveat: 3 linkage modes (S/S, N/N, S/N) x 2 geometrical isomers (cis/trans) = 6 isomers.

questions.questionText: A dextrorotatory optical isomer rotates plane-polarized light to the _______ and is denoted as ______.
questions.explanation: By standard convention in stereochemistry, a substance that rotates the plane of polarized light clockwise (to the right) is termed dextrorotatory and designated with the prefix "d-" or (+), whereas levorotatory rotates to the left and is designated "l-" or (-).
questions.notes: Dextrorotatory = right / d; Levorotatory = left / l.

questions.questionText: The complex ion [NiCl6]4- has a crystal field splitting parameter of 81 KJ/mol. Calculate its crystal field stabilization energy (CFFE).
questions.explanation: Ni2+ has a d8 electron configuration, giving the octahedral configuration t2g^6 eg^2. The CFSE is calculated as: CFSE = [6 * (-0.4) + 2 * (+0.6)] * Δo = -1.2 Δo. In magnitude, 1.2 * 81 kJ/mol = 97.2 kJ/mol, which rounds to 97 kJ/mol.
questions.notes: CFSE = 1.2 * 81 kJ/mol = 97.2 kJ/mol.

questions.questionText: Ethylenediamine is observed to form a more stable metal complex than methylamine. This is due to:
questions.explanation: Ethylenediamine is a bidentate chelating ligand that forms a stable five-membered chelate ring upon coordination. The chelate effect provides enhanced thermodynamic stability driven predominantly by a favorable increase in entropy (ΔS > 0) upon displacement of monodentate ligands.
questions.notes: Enhanced stability of multidentate over monodentate ligands is the chelate effect.

questions.questionText: What is the CFSE of low-spin d7 metal complex?
questions.explanation: A low-spin d7 octahedral complex has the configuration t2g^6 eg^1. The orbital energy contribution is 6(-0.4Δo) + 1(+0.6Δo) = -1.8Δo. In the spherical free-ion d7 ground state, there are 2 paired electrons and 3 unpaired electrons. In low-spin t2g^6 eg^1, there are 3 pairs, resulting in (3 - 2) = 1 extra electron pair. Accounting for pairing energy, CFSE = 1.8Δo - P.
questions.notes: Orbital stabilization is 1.8Δo with 1 net additional pairing energy penalty (-P).

questions.questionText: Which of the following on CO ligand is true?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide coordinates to transition metals through synergic bonding: it donates electron density from its HOMO (a carbon-centered σ lone pair) into empty metal d orbitals, while simultaneously accepting electron density from filled metal d orbitals into its empty LUMO (π* antibonding orbitals). Thus, CO is a σ-donor and π-acceptor.
questions.notes: Synergic bonding: sigma donation and pi back-acceptance.

questions.questionText: Which of the following metal complexes is expected to give the strongest Jahn-Teller effect?
questions.explanation: Jahn-Teller distortions are strongest when degenerate eg orbitals are asymmetrically populated, because eg lobes point directly along the metal-ligand bond axes. Low-spin d7 has the configuration t2g^6 eg^1, giving an unevenly occupied eg level and yielding a pronounced Jahn-Teller effect.
questions.notes: Low-spin d7 (eg1) has degenerate eg electrons pointing directly at ligands, driving strong distortion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following causes d-orbitals splitting in crystal field theory?
questions.explanation: In a purely spherical electrostatic field, all five d-orbitals remain degenerate. Degeneracy is lifted because metal d orbitals possess distinct spatial geometries and directional orientations: orbitals oriented along ligand directions experience greater electrostatic repulsion than those pointing between ligands.
questions.notes: Directional orientation of d-orbitals relative to incoming ligand charges drives crystal field splitting.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is not a coordination compound?
questions.explanation: 1,2-Diaminoethane (ethylenediamine) is an organic diamine that acts as a bidentate chelating ligand, rather than being a complete coordination compound itself. Transplatin, haemoglobin, and cobalt(III) ammines are all fully assembled coordination complexes.
questions.notes: 1,2-Diaminoethane is a free ligand, not a metal coordination complex.

questions.questionText: The number of chlorine atoms acting as counteranions in the complex [Co(en)2(H2)Cl]Cl2 is:
questions.explanation: In Werner-type formulas, species outside the square brackets serve as uncoordinated counterions balancing the charge. The formula [Co(en)2(H2)Cl]Cl2 explicitly places two chloride atoms outside the brackets, which act as counteranions in solution.
questions.notes: Two Cl- outside square brackets act as outer-sphere counteranions.

questions.questionText: Determine the number of structural isomers for the octahedral complex [Co(NH3)5CO3]Cl.
questions.explanation: The complex exhibits ionization isomerism through interchange of the inner-sphere carbonato ligand and outer-sphere chloride: [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]Cl and [Co(NH3)5Cl]CO3. Because pentaammine complexes have only one geometrical arrangement, there are exactly 2 structural isomers.
questions.notes: Pair of ionization isomers: [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]Cl and [Co(NH3)5Cl]CO3.
questions.caveat: Pair of ionization isomers: [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]Cl and [Co(NH3)5Cl]CO3.

questions.questionText: Which of the following compound shows only linkage isomerism?
questions.explanation: Nitrite is an ambidentate ligand capable of M-NO2 (nitro) and M-ONO (nitrito) binding. In [Co(NO2)(NH3)3]NO2, exchanging inner and outer anions gives the same composition, so it exhibits purely linkage isomerism without distinct ionization isomers.
questions.notes: Exclusive linkage isomerism via the nitro/nitrito ambidentate group.
questions.caveat: Exclusive linkage isomerism via the nitro/nitrito ambidentate group.

questions.questionText: A metal complex has a general formula of CoBr(NH3)5(SO4). What is the identity of this metal complex if it produces white precipitate when reacted with barium chloride?
questions.explanation: Addition of barium chloride tests for free sulfate counteranions in solution to precipitate insoluble white barium sulfate (BaSO4). Therefore, sulfate must reside in the outer coordination sphere as a counteranion, identifying the complex as [CoBr(NH3)5]SO4.
questions.notes: Outer-sphere SO4 2- precipitates with Ba2+ as white BaSO4.

questions.questionText: The name of the coordination compound K2[CoCl4] is:
questions.explanation: In systematic inorganic nomenclature, multiplying prefixes such as "di-" are not applied to simple counterions, ruling out A and B. The complex anion [CoCl4]2- carries a negative charge, requiring the suffix "-ate" as cobaltate(II), making potassium tetrachlorocobaltate(II) the correct IUPAC name.
questions.notes: No multiplying prefix on potassium; anionic complex requires -ate ending.

questions.questionText: The name of [Fe(CN)2((C6H5)3P)2] is:
questions.explanation: (C6H5)3P is triphenylphosphine, a neutral ligand that takes the multiplying prefix "bis-" because its name already contains a numerical descriptor ("tri-"). Two anionic cyanido ligands balance an iron(II) center in a neutral complex: dicyanobis(triphenylphosphine)iron(II).
questions.notes: Use bis- prefix for triphenylphosphine; oxidation state of Fe is +2.

questions.questionText: The name of [Cr(OH)4]- is:
questions.explanation: The ligand OH- is named hydroxo (or hydroxido). For an anionic complex, the metal name ends in "-ate" (chromate), and chromium's oxidation state is +3 (x + 4(-1) = -1 => x = +3), giving tetrahydroxochromate(III).
questions.notes: Hydroxo ligands; anionic complex takes -ate suffix (chromate(III)).

questions.questionText: Which of the following coordination complexes is most stable?
questions.explanation: The chelate effect provides enhanced thermodynamic stability to complexes containing polydentate ring-forming ligands compared to analogous monodentate systems due to favorable entropy changes. [Ni(en)3]2+ features three five-membered chelate rings, making it far more stable than the monodentate amine or aqua analogues.
questions.notes: Chelate effect greatly enhances stability of tris(ethylenediamine) complex.

questions.questionText: An oxalato ligand has four oxygen atoms. It is a
questions.explanation: Although the oxalate ion (C2O4 2-) contains four oxygen atoms, steric geometry and bite-angle constraints allow it to coordinate to a single metal center through only two oxygen donor atoms simultaneously, forming a stable five-membered chelate ring. It is therefore a bidentate ligand.
questions.notes: Oxalate coordinates via two carboxylate oxygen atoms (bidentate).

questions.questionText: Which of the following gives the least number of isomers?
questions.explanation: In [Ni(en)(NH3)4]2+, the bidentate ethylenediamine ligand can only span adjacent (cis) coordination sites, and all remaining four sites are occupied by identical monodentate NH3 ligands. Consequently, there is only 1 unique stereoisomer (no geometrical or optical isomers), giving the least number among all choices.
questions.notes: [Ni(en)(NH3)4]2+ has only a single isomer because en must coordinate cis.
questions.caveat: [Ni(en)(NH3)4]2+ has only a single isomer because en must coordinate cis.

questions.questionText: [Co(NH3)2(en)(NO2)2]Cl exhibits:

options.D: linkage, geometrical, optical and ionization isomerisms

questions.explanation: This complex contains ambidentate NO2- (giving linkage isomerism), outer-sphere Cl- with inner-sphere anions (giving ionization isomerism), non-equivalent ligands in octahedral geometry (giving cis/trans geometrical isomers), and chiral arrangements of the bidentate en and monodentate ligands (giving optical enantiomers). Hence, all four types are exhibited.
questions.notes: Exhibits linkage (NO2/ONO), ionization (NO2/Cl exchange), geometrical, and optical isomerism.
questions.caveat: Exhibits linkage (NO2/ONO), ionization (NO2/Cl exchange), geometrical, and optical isomerism.

questions.questionText: The total number of possible isomers for this metal complex [M(NO2)(SCN)(NH3)4] is:
questions.explanation: For an octahedral complex of type [Ma4bc], there are 2 geometrical isomers: cis and trans. Both NO2- (N or O donor) and SCN- (S or N donor) are ambidentate ligands with 2 linkage modes each. Multiplying the 2 geometrical forms by 2 (NO2/ONO) and 2 (SCN/NCS) gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 distinct structural/linkage isomers.
questions.notes: 2 geometrical arrangements (cis/trans) x 2 (NO2) x 2 (SCN) = 8 total isomers.
questions.caveat: 2 geometrical arrangements (cis/trans) x 2 (NO2) x 2 (SCN) = 8 total isomers.

questions.questionText: Which of the following compound shows optical isomerism?
questions.explanation: Tris-chelate octahedral complexes of the type [M(A-A)3], such as [Cr(en)3]3+, have D3 symmetry like a propeller and lack any improper axis of rotation (no plane of symmetry or center of inversion). They exist as stable, non-superimposable enantiomeric pairs (Δ and Λ), demonstrating optical isomerism.
questions.notes: [Cr(en)3]3+ is chiral (D3 propeller geometry) and shows optical activity.
questions.caveat: [Cr(en)3]3+ is chiral (D3 propeller geometry) and shows optical activity.

questions.questionText: The number of geometrical isomers shown by the octahedral complex of the type [M(A-B)3] is
questions.explanation: In an octahedral complex containing three identical unsymmetrical bidentate ligands [M(A-B)3], such as tris(glycinato)cobalt(III), there are exactly 2 geometrical isomers: the facial (fac) isomer, where like donor atoms occupy the corners of a triangular octahedral face, and the meridional (mer) isomer, where like donors define a meridian.
questions.notes: 2 geometrical isomers: fac and mer (each also possesses enantiomeric forms).
questions.caveat: 2 geometrical isomers: fac and mer (each also possesses enantiomeric forms).

questions.questionText: Which of the following metal atomic orbitals are considered in ligand field theory?
questions.explanation: Ligand Field Theory (LFT) adapts molecular orbital theory to transition metal complexes. It combines ligand group orbitals (LGOs) with all available metal valence atomic orbitals, which comprise the nd, (n+1)s, and (n+1)p orbitals (e.g. 3d, 4s, and 4p for first-row transition metals).
questions.notes: LFT utilizes metal s, p, and d valence orbitals in symmetry-adapted MO construction.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can lead to stronger metal-ligand bond?
questions.explanation: Metal-to-ligand π donation (π-backbonding) transfers electron density from filled metal d-orbitals into empty π* acceptor orbitals of ligands such as CO or CN-. This process operates synergistically with ligand-to-metal σ-donation, substantially strengthening and shortening the metal-ligand coordinate bond.
questions.notes: Synergistic metal-to-ligand pi backbonding strengthens the overall M-L bond.

questions.questionText: What causes the d-orbitals to lose their degeneracy in the ligand field theory?

options.C: mixing of metal atomic orbitals with ligand group orbitals

questions.explanation: In contrast to purely electrostatic CFT (which relies on point charges), Ligand Field Theory treats bonding via covalent orbital overlap. Degeneracy is lifted because metal atomic orbitals mix with symmetry-adapted Ligand Group Orbitals (LGOs), creating bonding, antibonding, and non-bonding molecular orbitals of differing energies.
questions.notes: LFT splits d-orbitals via covalent mixing with ligand group orbitals (LGOs).

questions.questionText: In [Ti(CO)6]4+, the Ti-C bond possesses:
questions.explanation: In [Ti(CO)6]4+, titanium is in the +4 oxidation state, which corresponds to a completely empty 3d0 electronic shell. Without valence d electrons, the metal cannot donate electron density back into the π* orbitals of CO, meaning the Ti-C bonding consists solely of σ-character from the carbonyl lone pair.
questions.notes: Ti(IV) has a d0 electron configuration, eliminating any possibility of pi backbonding.

questions.questionText: In the complex ion ML6 n+, Mn+ has six d-electrons and L is high field ligand. According to crystal field theory, how many unpaired electrons are there in this complex ion?
questions.explanation: A high-field ligand produces a large crystal field splitting (Δo > P), forcing electrons to pair in the lower-energy set before populating eg. For a d6 metal ion, all 6 electrons completely fill the t2g orbitals (configuration t2g^6 eg^0), resulting in zero unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).
questions.notes: Low-spin d6 in octahedral geometry is completely paired (t2g6, 0 unpaired).

questions.questionText: Which of the orbital will be most stablized if two axial ligands (i.e., along the z-axis) are removed?
questions.explanation: When the two axial ligands positioned along the z-axis of an octahedral complex are removed, electrostatic repulsion directly along the z-axis drops to zero. The dz2 orbital, which points head-on at the axial ligands, experiences the largest stabilization energy drop.
questions.notes: dz2 loses direct axial electrostatic ligand repulsion, dropping sharply in energy.

questions.questionText: What is the electronic arrangement of metal atom/ion in octahedral complex with d4 configuration, if Δo > pairing energy
questions.explanation: If Δo exceeds the pairing energy, electrons pair in the lower t2g set rather than promoting to the higher-energy eg set. For a d4 system, this leads to a low-spin configuration with all 4 electrons placed in t2g: t2g^4 eg^0.
questions.notes: Δo > P yields low-spin state (t2g4 eg0).

questions.questionText: The ratio of CFSE for [NiCl6]4- and [NiCl4]2- will be nearly:
questions.explanation: Both complexes feature Ni(II), a d8 ion. For octahedral [NiCl6]4-, CFSE_oct = 1.2 Δo. For tetrahedral [NiCl4]2- (configuration e^4 t2^4), CFSE_tet = 0.8 Δt. Using the geometric relationship Δt = (4/9)Δo, CFSE_tet = 0.8 * (4/9) Δo = (3.2/9) Δo. The ratio CFSE_oct / CFSE_tet is 1.2 / (3.2 / 9) = 10.8 / 3.2 = 27/8.

questions.questionText: The d orbitals that are stabilized in a tetrahedral magnetic field are:
questions.explanation: In a tetrahedral crystal field, the d-orbitals split inversely compared to octahedral geometry. The e orbitals (dx2-y2 and dz2) point toward the faces/edges of the cube rather than directly at the ligands, lying lower in energy and being stabilized by 0.6Δt below the barycenter.
questions.notes: In Td symmetry, the e set (dx2-y2, dz2) is stabilized relative to the barycenter.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is true when an octahedral metal complex undergoes axial compression?

options.A: dxy orbital has the lowest energy
options.B: dx2-y2 orbital has the highest energy
options.C: Metal d-orbitals with lobes pointing towards the Z axis are stablized

questions.explanation: In axial compression (z-in distortion), the two axial ligands move closer along the z-axis while the four equatorial ligands in the xy plane move outward. This outward relaxation in the xy plane stabilizes the in-plane orbitals; among the t2g set, the dxy orbital experiences the least repulsion and reaches the lowest energy.
questions.notes: Outward equatorial movement stabilizes dxy to the lowest energy level.

questions.questionText: Which of the following on fluoro ligand is true?
questions.explanation: Fluoride (F-) is an electronegative halide ion with filled valence p orbitals. It donates one lone pair via a σ-bond to the metal and additional electron density from its filled pπ orbitals into empty or half-filled metal t2g orbitals, classifying it as both a σ-donor and a π-donor.
questions.notes: Halide ligands like F- act as sigma-donors and pi-donors, reducing Δo.

questions.questionText: In the spectrochemical series, which ligand is neither a pi acceptor nor a pi donor?
questions.explanation: Ammonia (NH3) has only a single lone pair on the sp3-hybridized nitrogen atom, which it uses exclusively for σ-bonding. With no additional filled p orbitals (.
questions.notes: NH3 serves as the standard benchmark for pure sigma-donation in the spectrochemical series.
questions.caveat: unlike halides or water) and no low-energy empty π* antibonding orbitals (unlike CO or NO2-), NH3 is a pure σ-donor.

questions.questionText: Which effect/theory could account for the presence of two absorption peaks for a d1 metal complex?

options.D: Mixing of metal atomic orbitals and LGO

questions.explanation: In a d1 complex such as [Ti(H2O)6]3+, excitation of the single d electron promotes it from the t2g ground state to the eg level (t2g^0 eg^1). Because the eg state is electronically degenerate, it undergoes Jahn-Teller distortion that splits the eg level, resolving the d-d transition into two overlapping absorption peaks.
questions.notes: Excited state eg1 Jahn-Teller distortion splits the absorption band.

questions.questionText: In [Cu(H2O)6]2+, the original aqua ligands can be replaced by ammine ligands. Predict the major product.
questions.explanation: Due to the pronounced Jahn-Teller effect in Cu(II) (d9), the complex exhibits tetragonal elongation with four strongly bound equatorial bonds and two weakly bound elongated axial bonds. In aqueous ammonia, stepwise replacement readily substitutes the four equatorial aqua ligands to give [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ as the predominant stable species.
questions.notes: Jahn-Teller elongation causes a sharp drop in formation constant for the 5th and 6th ammonia ligands.

questions.questionText: When [Cr(CO)5(PH3)] is oxidized, what is the effect on the C-O bond?
questions.explanation: Oxidation increases the positive charge on the chromium center, contracting the metal d orbitals and reducing metal-to-CO π-backbonding. Because less electron density is donated into the antibonding π* orbitals of the carbonyl ligands, the C-O bond order increases, making the C-O bond stronger (and shorter).
questions.notes: Decreased backbonding into pi*(CO) strengthens and shortens the C-O triple bond.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a coordination compound?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is a neutral coordination complex featuring a central platinum(II) metal center coordinated by ammine and chlorido ligands. Platinum is an element, Fe2+ is a simple monatomic cation, and sulfuric acid is a covalent mineral acid.
questions.notes: Cisplatin is the prototypical neutral coordination complex.

questions.questionText: The central metal atom in [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] is:
questions.explanation: In [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], the ammine ligands are neutral (charge 0) and the two chloride ligands each carry a -1 charge. For a neutral complex, x + 2(0) + 2(-1) = 0, giving an oxidation state of +2 (Pt2+).
questions.notes: Standard square planar platinum(II) complex.

questions.questionText: Which of the following complexes can exhibit both geometrical and optical isomerism?

options.D: Both b and c are correct

questions.explanation: [Co(en)2Cl2]+ exists as cis and trans geometrical isomers. The cis isomer lacks an improper rotation axis and is chiral, existing as a pair of non-superimposable enantiomers (optical isomers), whereas [Cr(en)3]3+ has only optical (no geometrical) isomers.
questions.notes: cis-[Co(en)2Cl2]+ is chiral while trans is achiral; thus the complex exhibits both types.

questions.questionText: Which of the following compound shows only linkage isomerism?
questions.explanation: Nitrite is ambidentate, binding as nitro (-NO2) or nitrito (-ONO). In [Co(ONO)(NH3)3]NO2, exchanging the inner nitrito with outer nitrite produces an identical chemical entity, meaning it exhibits exclusively linkage isomerism.
questions.notes: Other options permit ionization or coordination sphere exchange.

questions.questionText: How many isomers are possible for the complex [Pt(NH3)(H2O)(SCN)(NO2)]
questions.explanation: A square planar complex [Mabcd] with four distinct ligands possesses 3 geometrical isomers. Here, two ligands are ambidentate: SCN- (2 modes: S, N) and NO2- (2 modes: N, O). Multiplying 3 geometrical arrangements by 2 (SCN/NCS) and by 2 (NO2/ONO) yields 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 distinct isomers.
questions.notes: 3 geometrical isomers x 2 linkage (SCN) x 2 linkage (NO2) = 12 total isomers.
questions.caveat: 3 geometrical isomers x 2 linkage (SCN) x 2 linkage (NO2) = 12 total isomers.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the correct name for [Cu(H2O)6][Pt(CN)6]:
questions.explanation: The cation is [Cu(H2O)6]2+ named hexaaquacopper(II). The counteranion must balance the +2 charge with a -2 charge, giving [Pt(CN)6]2-, where Pt is in the +4 oxidation state (x - 6 = -2 => x = +4), named hexacyanoplatinate(IV).
questions.notes: Anionic complex of platinum uses -ate suffix and roman numeral (IV).

questions.questionText: The name of [Fe(CN)2((CH3)3P)2] is:
questions.explanation: For complex ligand names containing prefixes or parentheses, such as trimethylphosphine, the multiplicative prefix "bis" is used instead of "di". Iron is in the +2 oxidation state (two anionic cyanides balance Fe2+), yielding dicyanobis(trimethylphosphine)iron(II).
questions.notes: Use bis- prefix for ligands with composite names like trimethylphosphine.

questions.questionText: Which of the following gives the highest number of isomers?
questions.explanation: [Cr(SCN)2(NH3)4]4+ combines cis and trans geometrical isomers with ambidentate linkage isomers for two SCN- ligands (cis/trans of -SCN/-SCN, -SCN/-NCS, and -NCS/-NCS), yielding the highest isomer multiplicity among the listed complexes.
questions.notes: Geometrical isomerism coupled with two ambidentate ligands generates the largest set of isomers.
questions.caveat: Geometrical isomerism coupled with two ambidentate ligands generates the largest set of isomers.

questions.questionText: What is the name for [Zn(OH)4]2-?
questions.explanation: The ligand OH- is designated as hydroxo (or hydroxido). Since the overall complex carries a 2- charge and four hydroxide ions (-4), the oxidation state of zinc is +2 (x - 4 = -2 => x = +2), and the anionic metal name takes the -ate suffix as zincate(II): tetrahydroxozincate(II).
questions.notes: Hydroxo ligand, zincate root with oxidation state +2.

questions.questionText: What is the name for Na2[Fe(C2O4)2(H2O)2]?
questions.explanation: The cation sodium is stated without multiplying prefix. Two oxalato ligands (C2O4 2-) carry a total charge of -4 and two neutral aqua ligands carry 0; to balance two Na+ cations (+2), iron must be in oxidation state +2 (x - 4 = -2 => x = +2), giving sodium diaquabis(oxalato)ferrate(II).
questions.notes: Oxidation state +2 on iron; anionic complex named ferrate.

questions.questionText: Which of the following metal atomic orbitals are considered in crystal field theory?
questions.explanation: Classical Crystal Field Theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model that focuses exclusively on the splitting of the five degenerate metal valence d-orbitals under the influence of an electric field generated by point-charge ligands, ignoring s and p orbital hybridization.
questions.notes: CFT treats only the d-orbitals as perturbed by the electrostatic ligand field; s and p are incorporated in Ligand Field / MO theory.

questions.questionText: What causes the metal d-orbitals to lose their degeneracy in the crystal field theory?

options.C: Repulsion between metal's d and p orbitals

questions.explanation: In CFT, ligands are modeled as point charges (or point dipoles) arranged in a specific geometry (e.g. octahedral or tetrahedral). The non-spherical, directional electrostatic repulsion from these point charges breaks the degeneracy of the metal d-orbitals.
questions.notes: Point charges at specific coordinate positions create the anisotropic field that splits d-orbitals.

questions.questionText: In [V(CO)6]5+, the V-C bond possesses:
questions.explanation: In [V(CO)6]5+, vanadium is in the +5 oxidation state, giving a d0 electronic configuration. Because there are no valence d electrons on V(V) to engage in π-backbonding into the empty π* orbitals of CO, the V-C interaction is limited strictly to σ-donation from the carbonyl ligands.
questions.notes: V(V) has a 3d0 configuration; with no d electrons available, metal-to-ligand pi backbonding cannot occur.

questions.questionText: Which of the orbital will be most stablized if two axial ligands (i.e., along the z-axis) are removed?
questions.explanation: Removing the two trans axial ligands along the z-axis transitions an octahedral complex into a square planar geometry. Because the dz2 orbital points directly along the z-axis, eliminating electrostatic repulsion from these ligands stabilizes dz2 more than any other orbital.
questions.notes: Removal of axial ligands relieves direct head-on electrostatic repulsion on dz2.

questions.questionText: What is the electronic arrangement of metal atom/ion in octahedral complex with d4 configuration? Assume pairing energy > Δo
questions.explanation: When pairing energy P > Δo, the energy cost to pair electrons in the t2g set exceeds the crystal field splitting energy, favoring a high-spin ground state. According to Hund's rule, three electrons enter t2g singly and the fourth promotes to eg, giving t2g^3 eg^1.
questions.notes: P > Δo defines the high-spin weak-field condition.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is true when an octahedral metal complex undergoes axial elongation?

options.A: dxy orbital has the lowest energy
options.B: dx2-y2 orbital has the highest energy
options.C: Metal d-orbitals with lobes pointing towards the Z axis are destablized

questions.explanation: In axial elongation (z-out distortion), the equatorial ligands in the xy plane are drawn slightly closer to compensate, maximizing repulsion with orbitals lying purely in the xy plane. Consequently, the dx2-y2 orbital rises to the highest energy level among all five d-orbitals.
questions.notes: Axial elongation lowers z-containing orbitals (dz2, dxz, dyz) and leaves dx2-y2 at highest energy.

questions.questionText: Which of the following on ammine ligand is true?
questions.explanation: Ammonia (NH3) acts purely as a σ-donor ligand through the lone pair on nitrogen. It has no low-lying empty π* orbitals to act as a π-acceptor and no additional lone pairs to act as a π-donor. Because it is a σ-donor only, "None of the above" is the correct choice.
questions.notes: NH3 is a classic pure sigma-donor ligand with no pi acid or pi base character.

questions.questionText: Identify the first-row transition metal M that satisfies the requirements given (more than one answer may be possible). [M(H2O)6]2+ having LFSE = 0.6Δo.
questions.explanation: Water is a weak-field ligand, giving high-spin complexes. For Cr2+ (d4 high-spin, t2g^3 eg^1), LFSE = 3(0.4) - 1(0.6) = 0.6Δo. For Cu2+ (d9, t2g^6 eg^3), LFSE = 6(0.4) - 3(0.6) = 0.6Δo. Therefore, both Cr and Cu satisfy the condition, making D correct.
questions.notes: Both high-spin d4 (Cr2+) and d9 (Cu2+) yield LFSE magnitude of 0.6Δo.

questions.questionText: What is the CFSE of a low-spin d6 metal complex?
questions.explanation: In a low-spin d6 octahedral complex, all 6 electrons reside in t2g: configuration t2g^6 eg^0, with 3 electron pairs. In the spherical free-ion ground state for d6, Hund's rule gives 1 paired electron and 4 unpaired electrons. The net increase in paired electrons is 3 - 1 = 2, so the CFSE is 2.4Δo - 2P (or stabilization with 2 extra pairing energies).
questions.notes: Low-spin d6 has two additional electron pairs beyond the free ion ground state (3 vs 1), leading to 2P in the CFSE expression.

questions.questionText: Which effect/theory could account for the presence of two absorption peaks for a d1 metal complex?
questions.explanation: For a d1 octahedral ion such as [Ti(H2O)6]3+, CFT predicts a single 2T2g -> 2Eg electronic transition.
questions.notes: Jahn-Teller distortion in the excited eg1 state splits the absorption peak into a doublet.
questions.caveat: However, the excited state (eg^1) has an unevenly filled eg set and undergoes significant Jahn-Teller distortion, splitting the eg level and producing two closely spaced absorption bands (or a split peak).

questions.questionText: Give the chemical name of [Fe(CN)2(CH3NH2)4].
questions.explanation: The neutral ligand CH3NH2 is methylamine, and the four methylamine ligands are named tetrakis(methylamine). The two cyanide ligands contribute a total charge of -2, so iron is in the +2 oxidation state in the neutral complex. The name is therefore dicyanotetrakis(methylamine)iron(II), corresponding to option D.
questions.notes: CH3NH2 is methylamine, not dimethylamine; four methylamine ligands require tetrakis(methylamine), and iron is in oxidation state +2.

questions.questionText: What is the coordination number of the metal center in KMnO4?
questions.explanation: In potassium permanganate (KMnO4), the permanganate anion MnO4- features a manganese(VII) center coordinated to four oxido ligands in a tetrahedral geometry. Therefore, the coordination number of manganese is 4.
questions.notes: Coordination number reflects the 4 surrounding oxido groups in the tetrahedral MnO4- anion.

questions.questionText: What is the oxidation state of the nickel metal centers in [Ni2Cl2(PPh3)2]?
questions.explanation: Neutral triphenylphosphine ligands (PPh3) contribute zero charge, while the two chloride ligands contribute a total of -2. For a neutral dinuclear complex [Ni2Cl2(PPh3)2], 2x + 2(-1) = 0, giving an average oxidation state of +1 for each nickel center.
questions.notes: Dinuclear nickel(I) species.

questions.questionText: Which of the following compound shows only linkage isomerism?
questions.explanation: Thiocyanate (SCN-) is an ambidentate ligand capable of coordinating via S or N. In [Co(NCS)(NH3)3]SCN, exchange of counterion does not yield a chemically distinct ionization isomer because the inner and outer ions are identical, so it exhibits only linkage isomerism.
questions.notes: Other options exhibit ionization or geometrical isomerism alongside linkage.
questions.caveat: Other options exhibit ionization or geometrical isomerism alongside linkage.

questions.questionText: How many isomers are possible for the complex [Pt(en)(NO3)(SCN)]?
questions.explanation: Platinum(II) complexes with coordination number 4 adopt square planar geometry. Because ethylenediamine is a chelating bidentate ligand occupying adjacent cis positions, no cis/trans geometrical isomerism is possible; only linkage isomerism of the ambidentate SCN- ligand (M-SCN vs M-NCS) gives 2 distinct isomers.
questions.notes: Chelating en prevents geometrical trans placement; 2 linkage isomers.
questions.caveat: Chelating en prevents geometrical trans placement; 2 linkage isomers.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the correct name for [Cu(H2O)6][Pt(CN)6]:
questions.explanation: The complex salt consists of the cation [Cu(H2O)6]2+ and the anion [Pt(CN)6]2-. Copper in aqueous hexaaqua is Cu(II), while Pt with six cyanides in a 2- anion has oxidation state +4 (x - 6 = -2 => x = +4), named hexacyanoplatinate(IV).
questions.notes: Cation named first, then anionic complex with -ate suffix.

questions.questionText: How many distinct isomers are possible for a metal complex containing three glycinato ligands?
questions.explanation: Glycinate is an unsymmetrical bidentate ligand (N,O donor, represented as A-B). An octahedral complex [M(A-B)3] has 2 geometrical isomers (facial and meridional), both of which are chiral and exist as enantiomeric pairs (Δ and Λ), resulting in a total of 4 stereoisomers.
questions.notes: Facial and meridional isomers each have a non-superimposable mirror image (2 x 2 = 4 stereoisomers).
questions.caveat: Facial and meridional isomers each have a non-superimposable mirror image (2 x 2 = 4 stereoisomers).

questions.questionText: Which of the following gives the highest number of isomers?
questions.explanation: [Cr(SCN)2(NH3)4]4+ (often written with ambidentate SCN-) possesses both cis/trans geometrical isomerism and multiple linkage combinations (SCN/SCN, SCN/NCS, NCS/NCS), generating the highest total number of isomers among the choices.
questions.notes: Combination of cis/trans geometrical and multiple linkage modes yields the greatest count.

questions.questionText: Which of the following tetrahedral metal complex shows optical isomerism? M denotes a metal center. A, B, C, and D indicate different types of donor atom. A hypen "-" indicates bond between donor atoms (i.e., multidentate ligand).
questions.explanation: A tetrahedral complex lacks a center of inversion or plane of symmetry when all four coordinated donor atoms are distinct or arranged asymmetrically. Complex [M(A-B)(C-D)] has four non-equivalent coordination sites without an improper rotation axis Sn, rendering it chiral and optically active.
questions.notes: Asymmetrical chelate coordination in tetrahedral geometry removes symmetry planes.

questions.questionText: What is the name for Na2[Fe(C2O4)2(H2O)2]?
questions.explanation: In IUPAC naming, counterions do not use numerical prefixes (hence "sodium", not "disodium"). Because the coordination entity is an anion [Fe(C2O4)2(H2O)2]2-, the iron metal takes the suffix "-ate" as ferrate(II), arranged alphabetically: diaquabis(oxalato)ferrate(II).
questions.notes: No multiplying prefix on simple cation counterion; anionic complex uses ferrate.

questions.questionText: In ligand field theory, which of the following metal atomic orbitals are used for sigma bonding with ligands in an octahedral complex ?
questions.explanation: In octahedral symmetry (Oh), the ligand donor lone pairs point directly along the Cartesian axes (x, y, z). Only metal orbitals with eg symmetry pointing directly along these axes (dx2-y2 and dz2), along with s (a1g) and p (t1u) orbitals, participate in σ-bonding.
questions.notes: The t2g set (dxy, dyz, dxz) points between axes and is strictly non-bonding with respect to sigma interactions.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statement indicates a stable metal complex?
questions.explanation: A thermodynamically stable metal complex is characterised by a high formation constant (Kf), a low dissociation constant (Kd = 1/Kf), and strong metal-ligand binding affinity. Since options A, B, and C all describe unstable complexes, D ("None of the above") is the correct statement.
questions.notes: High Kf and low Kd correspond to stability; options A-C all indicate instability.

questions.questionText: In the metal complex [Zn(F)6]4-, what type of bonding interaction(s) is/are present in the Zn-F bond?

options.C: Both ligand-to-metal and metal-to-ligand π characters

questions.explanation: Zn2+ has a completely filled d10 electronic configuration. Because its d orbitals are fully occupied, it cannot accept π donation from fluoride into its d-shell, nor does fluoride possess low-lying empty π* orbitals for backbonding, making the bonding predominantly σ in character.
questions.notes: Zn(II) d10 configuration limits metal-ligand orbital overlap primarily to sigma interactions in this question model.

questions.questionText: Which of the orbital will be most destablized when we convert a square planar metal complex into a square pyramidal metal complex by adding one additional ligand to the metal complex?
questions.explanation: Adding an axial ligand along the z-axis introduces direct electrostatic repulsion and orbital overlap along the z direction. The dz2 orbital, which points directly along the z-axis, experiences the greatest increase in energy and is therefore most destabilized.
questions.notes: Direct approach of axial ligand destabilizes dz2 significantly compared to in-plane orbitals.

questions.questionText: What is the electronic arrangement of metal atom/ion in octahedral metal complex with d4 configuration? Assume pairing energy < Δo
questions.explanation: When pairing energy P < Δo, the crystal field splitting is larger than the energy required to pair electrons, resulting in a low-spin complex. For a d4 ion, all 4 electrons populate the lower-energy t2g orbitals, giving the configuration t2g^4 eg^0.
questions.notes: P < Δo favors pairing in lower t2g set (low-spin state).

questions.questionText: Which of the following octahedral metal complex exhibits the strongest Jahn-Teller effect?
questions.explanation: The Jahn-Teller effect is strongest when the degenerate eg orbitals are unevenly occupied, because eg orbitals point directly at the ligands. High-spin d4 has the configuration t2g^3 eg^1, featuring an asymmetrically occupied eg set and resulting in a strong Jahn-Teller distortion.
questions.notes: Uneven eg occupancy (eg1 or eg3) yields pronounced geometric distortion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following on phosphine ligand is true?
questions.explanation: Tertiary phosphines (PR3) donate a lone pair from phosphorus via a σ-bond to the metal and accept electron density from filled metal d orbitals into low-lying empty σ*(P-R) orbitals (π-backbonding). Thus, phosphines act as σ-donors and π-acceptors.
questions.notes: PR3 donates via P lone pair and accepts into sigma*(P-C/P-R) orbitals.

questions.questionText: Identify the first-row transition metal M that satisfies the requirements given (more than one answer may be possible). K2[MF4] having half-filled doubly degenerate e orbitals.
questions.explanation: In K2[MF4], the complex anion is tetrahedral [MF4]2-, so the metal M is in the +2 oxidation state. In a tetrahedral field, the lower set is the doubly degenerate e set (e^2 is half-filled). For Ti2+ (a d2 transition metal), both electrons occupy the e set: e^2 t2^0, giving half-filled doubly degenerate e orbitals.
questions.notes: Ti(II) is 3d2. In tetrahedral [TiF4]2-, e orbitals are half-filled (e2).

questions.questionText: What is the CFSE of a d8 octahedral metal complex?
questions.explanation: An octahedral d8 complex has the configuration t2g^6 eg^2 regardless of field strength. The CFSE is calculated as: [6 * (-0.4) + 2 * (+0.6)] Δo = -1.2Δo. Expressed as stabilization magnitude without changing the pairing energy relative to free ion, it equals 1.2Δo.
questions.notes: CFSE magnitude = 1.2Δo; pairing energy correction is zero relative to spherical field for d8.

questions.questionText: The aqua ligands of [Cu(H2O)6]2+ can be replaced by ammine ligands. Which of the following is expected to be the major product?
questions.explanation: Cu(II) is a d9 system with strong Jahn-Teller elongation along the z-axis. The four equatorial water ligands are tightly bound and readily replaced by ammonia, but the two elongated axial positions remain occupied by weaker water molecules in aqueous solution, yielding [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ as the predominant product.
questions.notes: Jahn-Teller axial elongation prevents easy replacement of the 5th and 6th axial ligands in water.
